content.title: About
content.content: Beans and rice with tomatoes is a classic dish that combines protein‑rich beans, carbohydrate‑dense rice, and flavorful tomatoes. It is popular in many cuisines where simple, hearty, and nutritious meals are valued.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beans are an excellent source of plant protein and fiber.
Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that gives them their bright red color.
The bean‑rice combination provides a complete set of essential amino acids.
The dish can be easily adapted with different spices, vegetables, or meats.
Tomatoes help improve iron absorption from beans.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beans supply plant protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Fiber and potassium in beans and rice help regulate cholesterol and blood pressure.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene and vitamin C from tomatoes protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Steady energy release
items.content: Complex carbohydrates in rice release glucose slowly, providing lasting satiety.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Fiber from beans and tomatoes promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in excess.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Legumes can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people; soaking beans before cooking helps.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the dish is prepared with added salt or sauces, monitor overall sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course or as a side. It stores well in the refrigerator and can be reheated. Enhance flavor with fresh herbs, spices, a drizzle of olive oil, or a sprinkle of cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before consuming.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef tongue is a muscular, rich cut from the tongue of cattle, with a firm texture and a rich, beefy flavor. It is tough when raw but becomes tender and succulent when simmered or braised for a long time. Beef tongue is eaten in many cuisines, in dishes such as tacos de lengua, sandwiches, stews, and cold cuts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef tongue is a muscle meat, not an organ meat in the strict sense, though it is classed as offal.
It is cooked slowly and the tough outer skin is peeled off after cooking.
It is a traditional dish in Latin American, Eastern European, Jewish, and Asian cuisines.
Tongue is a fatty, well-marbled cut with a smooth, tender texture when cooked.
It can be served hot, sliced cold, pickled, or smoked.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef tongue provides complete protein for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Provides zinc and iron
items.content: Zinc supports immune function, and heme iron is readily absorbed.

items.title: Provides other B vitamins and selenium
items.content: Beef tongue contains niacin, riboflavin, vitamin B6, and selenium.

items.title: Rich and filling
items.content: Tongue is a satisfying, flavorful cut.

items.title: High in fat and calories
items.content: Tongue is a fatty cut and is calorie-dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Cholesterol and saturated fat
items.content: Tongue contains cholesterol and saturated fat, so people limiting these should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Sodium in cured products
items.content: Pickled, corned, or smoked tongue can be very high in sodium.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Cook thoroughly and keep raw tongue separate from other foods.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beef tongue is usually simmered for several hours with onion, garlic, and herbs until tender, then the outer skin is peeled off and the meat is sliced. It can be served hot with sauce, in tacos, or sandwiches, or chilled and thinly sliced. It can also be braised or pressure-cooked.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw tongue in the refrigerator and cook it within one to two days, or freeze it for longer storage. Cooked tongue should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to four days, or frozen. Cured tongue should be stored according to its package instructions.

chicken-thigh-baked-coated-skin-coating-.title: Chicken thigh, baked, coated, skin/coating eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh is the dark meat from the upper part of a bird's leg. When baked in the oven with a coating (breaded, sauced or marinated), it stays juicy while the crispy crust adds flavor and texture. The skin and coating are edible and often contain additional taste components.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark meat contains more iron and zinc than white meat.
Baking with a coating helps retain moisture, making the meat more tender.
Chicken thighs are used in many traditional dishes, from French confit to Asian teriyaki.
The skin provides beneficial fats but also contributes cholesterol.
When properly cooked, the skin becomes crunchy and aromatic, a favorite element in many recipes.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat contains vitamin B6, niacin and riboflavin, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Thigh meat supplies iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Selenium and vitamin B6 help maintain a normal immune response.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Fats in the skin and coating provide a quick source of energy, especially during high physical activity.

items.title: High fat and cholesterol
items.content: Skin and coating increase saturated fat content, so people with cardiovascular disease should limit intake.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked meat may contain Salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

items.title: Allergy to coating ingredients
items.content: Breadings can contain dairy, gluten or nuts, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salty sauces and marinades can raise sodium levels, which is undesirable for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Baked coated chicken thighs are convenient hot or cold—in salads, sandwiches or as a main dish. The skin and coating can be eaten together with the meat, adding crunch and flavor. Serve in bite‑size pieces for easy consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked tuna is the flesh of the marine fish after thermal processing (usually boiling or steaming). Tuna belongs to the Scombridae family, has a firm texture, mild flavor, and is rich in protein. It is commonly used in salads, sandwiches, and Asian dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna can grow over 300 kg and is one of the largest bony fishes.
Tuna meat is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, which are beneficial for heart health.
Canned tuna is one of the most popular food products worldwide.
In Japan, cooked tuna (often served as sashimi) is considered a delicacy, although it is traditionally eaten raw.
Tuna can migrate long distances, sometimes over 5,000 km in search of food.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Cooked tuna provides about 30 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA in tuna support cardiovascular health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Compared with many other fish, cooked tuna has a relatively low total fat content, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna is a good source of vitamin B12, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains selenium, magnesium, and potassium, essential for nerve function and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Tuna can accumulate mercury; pregnant women and young children should limit consumption.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including tuna.

items.title: Processing and canning
items.content: Long‑term storage in cans can increase sodium levels, so monitor salt intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked tuna can be diced for salads, added to pasta, used in sandwiches, or served with vegetable sides. It can also be quickly pan‑seared after boiling to create a golden crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked tuna in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if any are present.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen coffee drink, nonfat is a refreshing beverage made from cold coffee without any added dairy fat. It contains caffeine, flavorings and sweeteners, but virtually no calories or fat, making it popular among weight‑watchers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink is often served as a granita or frozen cubes that melt in the mouth, creating a light foam.
Lack of fat preserves a brighter coffee flavor without buttery notes.
In many countries it is sold in ready‑to‑drink plastic cups that can be microwaved.
Caffeine content is comparable to regular cold coffee – about 80‑100 mg per 250 ml.
Vanilla, caramel or cinnamon extracts are sometimes added to enhance taste.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols, which help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Boosts alertness
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving concentration and reducing fatigue.

items.title: Supports metabolism
items.content: Caffeine may increase metabolic rate, aiding calorie burning.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The absence of fat makes the drink virtually calorie‑free, suitable for diet plans.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: As a liquid beverage, it contributes to overall water balance.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: People sensitive to caffeine may experience anxiety, insomnia or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Sweetener content
items.content: Some versions use artificial sweeteners that can cause discomfort in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Cold shock
items.content: Consuming a very cold drink may cause tooth or throat discomfort for those with sensitive enamel.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine can amplify the effects of certain medications, such as stimulants or antidepressants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the frozen coffee drink, nonfat right after thawing to keep its refreshing character. It can be blended into smoothies, used as a cocktail base, or topped with nonfat whipped cream for a smoother taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the product in a freezer at –18 °C or lower. Once opened, consume within 1‑2 weeks to prevent crystal formation and flavor changes.

rice-brown-with-carrots-and-tomatoes-and.title: Brown Rice with Carrots and Tomatoes

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain rice that retains its bran layer and germ. In this dish it is cooked together with carrots and tomatoes or a tomato‑based sauce, making it flavorful and nutritious.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice provides more fiber, vitamins, and minerals than white rice.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Tomatoes are a good source of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
The combination of tomatoes and carrots gives the dish a bright color and natural sweetness.
When stored properly, whole‑grain rice can keep its quality for up to a year.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Brown rice releases energy slowly, providing sustained fuel throughout the day.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Carrots and tomatoes add vitamin A, vitamin C, potassium, and iron to the dish.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and beta‑carotene from carrots help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Fiber and potassium contribute to healthy blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to rice.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals if consumed in excess.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Tomatoes contain oxalates; people prone to kidney stones should consume them in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish as a side to meat, fish, or legumes. It also works well in salads, soups, or as a base for vegetarian meals. Add herbs, spices, or nuts for extra flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Dry brown rice should be stored in a cool, dry place in a sealed package for up to 12 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried rice with shrimp is an Asian dish where cooked rice is stir‑fried with shrimp, vegetables and soy sauce. It offers a fragrant flavor that balances the tenderness of seafood with the mild sweetness of rice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is popular in China, Thailand and Vietnam, often served as a quick lunch or snack.
Long‑grain rice is traditionally used because it stays separate during frying.
Shrimp are usually marinated in soy sauce, ginger and garlic before cooking.
Variations may include pineapple, cashews or chili for extra heat.
It is commonly prepared in a wok, a deep pan that allows high‑heat, fast cooking.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide a lean, easily digestible source of protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When cooked with minimal oil, fried rice with shrimp contains little saturated fat compared with many other fried dishes.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: Both rice and shrimp supply B‑vitamins such as B6 and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Shrimp are rich in selenium, zinc and iodine, nutrients important for immune function and thyroid health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Soy sauce and ginger add antioxidant compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp can trigger severe allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce is high in salt; people with hypertension should limit its amount.

items.title: Foodborne toxins
items.content: Improperly stored shrimp may harbor bacteria that cause food poisoning.

items.title: Portion control
items.content: The dish can become calorie‑dense if a lot of oil is used; moderation is key.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, garnished with sliced green onions or cilantro. It is easy to eat with a fork or spoon, and pairs well with extra vegetable sides or a fresh salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat with a splash of oil or water to restore moisture.

rice-white-with-dark-green-vegetables-fa.title: White Rice with Dark Green Vegetables, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of boiled white rice, sautéed dark green vegetables (such as broccoli or spinach), and a small amount of added vegetable fat. The combination of carbohydrates, fiber, and fats makes it nutritious and satisfying.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple food for more than half of the world’s population.
Dark green vegetables are rich in chlorophyll, which gives them their characteristic color and flavor.
Adding a modest amount of fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins from the vegetables.
Such combinations are traditional in Asian cuisines, where rice and vegetables are often cooked with oil or sesame oil.
When balanced correctly, a serving can provide roughly 400–500 kcal.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbohydrates.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: White rice contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Fiber and antioxidants
items.content: Dark green vegetables supply fiber, vitamin K, vitamin C, and antioxidants that support heart health and immunity.

items.title: Enhanced nutrient absorption
items.content: Fat aids the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K from the vegetables.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: The rice‑vegetable combo promotes regular bowel movements thanks to fiber and the probiotic potential of some greens.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If seasoned with soy sauce or other salty additives, the sodium level may be high.

items.title: Allergy to vegetable oils
items.content: Some individuals may react to the type of oil used (e.g., peanut oil).

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Added fat increases calorie count, so portions should be controlled in weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a side or a main course. It pairs well with soy sauce, spices, or fresh herbs. It also complements chicken, fish, or tofu.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat with a splash of water or a little oil to prevent drying out.
